extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of Old English literature; translators and editors of Beowulf
extracted.subtask_description: Scholarly edition notes and emendation guidance for translating and editing Beowulf, discussing variant readings, grammatical parsing, glossary consistency, and interpretive options for difficult passages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resolve ambiguous pronoun referents and preserve rhetorical contrasts
rubrics_metrics.description: One crux is to find out _whose head_ is meant; another is to bring out the antithesis between 'head' and 'hand.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a line is ambiguous about referents (e.g., whose 'head' is meant), choose readings or punctuation that clarify the referent and preserve poetic antithesis or rhetorical contrasts. Translator/editors should note the crux and prefer interpretations that strengthen the poem's rhetorical effect rather than produce confusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emend pleonastic or repetitive conjunctions to improve sense and flow
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Þæt þæt fýr' (2702), S. emends to 'þá þæt fýr' = when the fire began to grow less intense afterward. This emendation relieves the passage of a plethora of conjunctive _þæt_'s.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If original wording produces awkward repetition (a 'plethora' of the same particle), consider emendation to a more felicitous particle that restores sense and syntactic clarity. Note and justify such emendations in apparatus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer emendations that yield coherent syntax and plausible meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: For 'gefyldan' (2707), S. proposes 'gefylde.' ... This gives Beowulf the credit of having felled the dragon; then they combine to annihilate him. The reading 'life drove out strength' is very unsatisfactory and very peculiar. I would suggest as follows: Adopt S.'s emendation, remove H.'s parenthesis, read 'ferh-ellen wræc,' and translate: 'He felled the foe, drove out his life-strength' (that is, made him hors de combat).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where literal manuscript readings yield implausible or 'very unsatisfactory' meanings, prefer emendations that produce coherent syntax and plausible action within the poem (e.g., giving Beowulf credit for a deed). Explain alternatives and why the chosen emendation is preferable.

rubrics_metrics.name: When a word is vague, present alternative senses and pick translation consistent with tone
rubrics_metrics.description: The word 'oferhígian' (2767) being vague and little understood, two quite distinct translations of this passage have arisen. One takes 'oferhígian' as meaning 'to exceed'... The other takes 'oferhígian' as meaning 'to render arrogant,' and, giving the sentence a moralizing tone, renders substantially as in the body of this work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: List plausible senses for obscure words and indicate how each choice affects tone (e.g., descriptive vs moralizing). Prefer the sense that best fits wider context and register; record alternative renderings in notes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flag and discuss disputed referents or object identities in contested passages
rubrics_metrics.description: The passage beginning here is very much disputed. 'The bill of the old lord' is by some regarded as Beowulf's sword; by others, as that of the ancient possessor of the hoard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For passages where the identity of an object/person is disputed, present the competing readings and their textual/syntactic bases. Explain implications for meaning and, if necessary, leave conjectural ambiguity in text while discussing preferred reading in footnote.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make internal editorial apparatus consistent (text, notes, glossary)
rubrics_metrics.description: Several discrepancies and other oversights have been noticed in the H.-So. glossary. ... As, however, this book may fall into the hands of some who have no copy of the American edition, it seems best to notice all the principal oversights of the German editors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure glossary entries, textual notes, and main text agree. If earlier editions contain conflicting glosses or grammatical assignments, correct them and document corrections in Addenda so readers without other editions are not misled.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide grammatical parsing and case assignments with emendatory suggestions
rubrics_metrics.description: For 'góda,' B. suggests 'gomela.' ... 'Hige-méðum' (2910) is glossed by H. as dat. plu. (= for the dead). S. proposes 'hige-méðe,' nom. sing. limiting Wigláf; i.e. W., mood-weary, holds head-watch o'er friend and foe.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where morphology or syntax is doubtful, propose parsings (case, number) and alternative readings; explain how each parsing affects translation. Record which critic supports which parsing and justify the editor's choice.

rubrics_metrics.name: When meaning depends on punctuation or compounding, consider emendation of word-division or punctuation
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Ær gescód' (2778), translated in this work as verb and adverb, is by some regarded as a compound participial adj. = sheathed in brass. ... 'nihtes' and 'hwílum' (3045) as separate adverbial cases vs. combined sense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Punctuation, compounding, or morphological interpretation can change sense; editors should evaluate whether to treat forms as separate words, compounds, or different parts of speech and justify the punctuation/emendation adopted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer readings that avoid gratuitous parenthetical constructions unless manuscript compels them
rubrics_metrics.description: Remove H.'s parenthesis, read 'ferh-ellen wræc,' ... The parenthesis is by some emended so as to read: (1) (He (i.e. God) is the hope of men); (2) (he is the hope of heroes). Gr.'s reading has no parenthesis, but says: ... The last is rejected on many grounds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If parenthetical punctuation in transmission creates ambiguity, favor readings without parenthesis when they yield clearer syntax and are supported by context or other manuscript/critical evidence; note rejected parenthetical readings and reasons.

rubrics_metrics.name: When multiple scholarly interpretations exist, record them and indicate preferred one with reasons
rubrics_metrics.description: The name 'Scyldingas' here (3006) has caused much discussion, and given rise to several theories, the most important of which are as follows: (1) After the downfall of Hrothgar's family, Beowulf was king of the Danes... (2) For 'Scyldingas' read 'Scylfingas'... (3) M. considers 3006 a thoughtless repetition... Cf. H.-So.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: List competing theories for difficult proper names/terms and evaluate plausibility. State the editor's preferred interpretation and provide textual or contextual reasons; leave alternative theories in apparatus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Translate archaisms and idioms with attention to register and the poem's overall tone
rubrics_metrics.description: B. takes 'nihtes' and 'hwílum' (3045) as separate adverbial cases, and renders: Joy in the air had he of yore by night, etc. He thinks that the idea of vanished time ought to be expressed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When rendering archaic adverbials or idiomatic phrases, consider the poem's temporal perspective and tone (e.g., 'of yore', 'by night'); choose translations that preserve poetic sense and temporal coloring rather than literal word order alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Document and justify all editorial emendations and variant readings in notes
rubrics_metrics.description: Numerous suggested emendations (e.g., 'gehýdde' vs 'gehýðde', 'forgifan' case assignments, 'brád' vs 'brún-ecg') are listed with reasons and references to critics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Every emendation or change from the base text should be documented, with competing readings and critic attributions given. Provide succinct rationale so users understand why the editor preferred one reading over others.
